final_answer:
PRIVILEGED DRAFT - ANTITRUST RISK ASSESSMENT AND HSR FILING STRATEGY
Crescent Fund IV (TGD Acquisition Corp.) / Triton Industrial Gas Distribution, Inc.
To: Ashford, Kendrick & Hale deal team. Basis: the nine deal documents supplied; law checked October 2, 2026. Deal timeline follows the documents (SPA signed April 14, 2025; HSR filing due April 28, 2025).

1. BOTTOM LINE
- A Second Request is likely and an enforcement challenge or consent decree is the base case. On any version of the numbers, Hattiesburg, Gulfport-Biloxi and Baton Rouge exceed the 2023 Merger Guidelines presumption. Medical and specialty gases are separate-market problems that the deal team's headline figures (26.4% overall, 20.6% medical) obscure.
- The record is internally inconsistent (narrative shares and HHIs versus the market-data workbook). Reconcile it before anything goes to an agency.
- The $40M divestiture cap fits a Mississippi-plus-Mobile package but not Louisiana. The reverse-fee and termination architecture gives Crescent a cheap exit, leaves gaps, and the Aug. 1 / Oct. 31, 2025 timetable is unrealistic if a Second Request issues.
-

2. HSR MECHANICS - CORRECTIONS
(a) Threshold and fee. The IC memo, Triton board deck, Bledsoe prior-acquisitions memo and SPA s.6.3(b) use a $119.5M threshold and a $160,000 fee ("$161.5M-$500M tier"). $119.5M was the 2024 threshold. Effective Feb. 21, 2025 the threshold is $126.4M; size-of-person is $252.9M/$25.3M; the fee for $179.4M to under $555.5M is $105,000. No 2025 tier is $160,000, so $55,000 would be overpaid and the documents' reliability is in question. SPA s.6.3(b) ("or such other amount") cures the contract.
(b) Reportability. Consideration of at least $310M cash (plus earnout fair value; target debt repaid at closing counts, debt that merely stays outstanding generally does not - confirm) exceeds $126.4M but is below the roughly $505.8M level, so size-of-person applies. It is met (Triton sales $274M; acquiring person at least $25.3M). "$2.8B committed capital" is not the test; use the acquiring person's actual balance sheet.
(c) Acquiring person. Praxion sits in Fund III; the buyer is Fund IV. Who is the UPE (16 C.F.R. 801.1) decides whose officers' documents, overlaps and prior acquisitions must be reported. The documents treat Crescent Capital Partners as UPE, and SPA s.6.4(g) represents Crescent can compel Praxion to remedy. Treat the entities consistently; the agencies will treat Praxion and Triton as commonly controlled under Clayton s.7 regardless.
(d) Form. The IC memo and Bledsoe memo describe a 10-year lookback; the final rule kept a five-year lookback and $10M sales/assets threshold for prior acquisitions. Delta Cylinder (Mar. 2022, $12M) and Coastal Air & Gas (Sept. 2023, $8.5M) fall inside five years; confirm Coastal exceeded $10M. The new form also requires overlap descriptions, Item 4(c)/4(d) documents, a supervisory-deal-team-lead's documents and CEO-level plans and reports. That rule was vacated in Chamber of Commerce v. FTC, No. 6:25-cv-9-JDK (E.D. Tex. Feb. 12, 2026); the Fifth Circuit denied a stay on Mar. 19, 2026 and the FTC reverted to the prior form (appeal status unverified). An April 2025 filing used the new form; any refiling today would use the old form. Either way, assume every document below is produced, because a Second Request sweeps them in.
(e) Timing. Ten business days (Apr. 28) is tight for the new form; missing it breaches s.6.3(a) and, under s.8.1(e)(iii), forfeits the outside-date extension right. A filing on Apr. 28 starts a 30-day waiting period (expires about May 28, 2025). Pull-and-refile (SPA s.6.3(g)) buys one further 30 days; a Second Request extends review until 30 days after substantial compliance.

3. SUBSTANTIVE RISK
3.1 Standard. Clayton Act s.7 (15 U.S.C. s.18) bars acquisitions that may substantially lessen competition in any line of commerce in any section of the country. Binding authority: United States v. Philadelphia National Bank, 374 U.S. 321 (1963) (30% share presumption); United States v. Baker Hughes, 908 F.2d 981 (D.C. Cir. 1990) (burden-shifting). The 2023 Merger Guidelines are persuasive, not binding, but the FTC and DOJ announced on Feb. 18, 2025 that they remain in effect. Guideline 1 presumes illegality if post-merger HHI exceeds 1,800 with a change above 100, or if the merged share exceeds 30% with a change above 100. Pinnacle and the Praxion deck instead use 2,500/200, which is the older approach; the correct thresholds are lower and catch more markets. State attorneys general (LA, MS, AL) may sue independently.

3.2 Markets. Local MSA geographic markets are likely (delivery economics; Pinnacle says a 100-150 mile radius, the Triton deck says 150-250 - reconcile). Statewide figures (26.4% of $1,070M) are legally irrelevant. Bulk, packaged, specialty and medical gases should each be assumed to be separate product markets. Medical is the sharpest problem: the workbook shows Hattiesburg and Gulfport-Biloxi going from three FDA/state-licensed suppliers (Praxion, Triton, Linde) to two, with 6-18 month licensing barriers. A divestiture buyer would need existing licenses.

3.3 The numbers do not reconcile.
MSA | IC/Pinnacle bulk combined share; delta HHI | Workbook revenue-derived bulk share; delta HHI | Other workbook shares
Baton Rouge | 42%; 864 | 37.8%; 662 | specialty 36.8%, packaged 33.3%
New Orleans | 38%; 690 | 25.2%; 311 | specialty 32.5%
Gulfport-Biloxi | 52%; 1,280 | 42.2%; 846 | specialty 56.2%, packaged 51.3%
Hattiesburg | 61%; 1,848 | 37.3%; 687 | specialty 46.0%, packaged 39.0%
Mobile | 28%; 360 | 19.7%; 191 | medical 19.1%
The workbook's HHI columns repeat the narrative figures, which its own revenue columns contradict. Other conflicts: Pinnacle counts 17 overlap-MSA branches and about $172M of revenue (average-branch method), but the workbook lists 23 branches and $230.3M actual (Praxion $119.2M, Triton $111.1M).
Pinnacle's HHI arithmetic is also unreliable. From its own Appendix A-1 shares, pre-merger HHIs are at most about 1,792 (Baton Rouge), 1,732 (New Orleans), 2,026 (Gulfport-Biloxi) and 1,774 (Mobile), below the reported 2,150/1,980/2,480/1,850. Hattiesburg's reported 2,141 is impossible because the three named firms alone give 2,357 (28, 33 and 22 percent squared), implying a post-merger HHI of at least 4,205. New Orleans and Mobile turn on which data set is right; Hattiesburg, Gulfport-Biloxi and Baton Rouge trip the 30%/100 test on both.

3.4 Customers. Praxion and Triton share about 20 customers with $121.4M combined spend ($71.1M is 25.9% of Triton revenue). PetroStar combined spend is $30.5M (Triton $22.0M plus Praxion $8.5M), not $22M; Gulf Coast Shipbuilders is $20.2M, not $14M. Many are rated "HIGH/VERY HIGH" switching cost, dual-source "for pricing leverage" and have contracts expiring 2025-26 (e.g., Magnolia Steel, Biloxi Regional, Ingalls). These customers will be the agencies' witnesses.

3.5 Precedent. Pinnacle, the Triton deck and the IC memo describe Linde/Praxair as a "2019" action requiring distribution divestitures in "seven MSAs." The FTC consent (Oct. 2018) required divestitures in nine industrial gas markets, mostly upstream assets (air separation units, CO2, helium, hydrogen) to Messer and Matheson. It does not support "substantially similar facts." The better precedent is Air Liquide/Airgas (FTC, 2016): local geographic markets, including retail packaged welding gas and hardgoods stores, remedied by divesting stores. Pinnacle's "2022 DOJ Midwest clearance" and its claim that the FTC has recognized specialty gases as a market could not be verified; do not cite them to an agency. Pinnacle's quoted Merger Guidelines language on serial acquisitions is unverified; cite Guideline 8 directly after checking.

3.6 Hot documents (all likely responsive to Item 4(c)/4(d) or a Second Request). IC memo: "eliminate duplicative competitive pressure," "optimize pricing," "set market-appropriate pricing," branch closures that "reduce the intensity of local competition." Rennick to Dunleavy, Dec. 15, 2024: "stop the pricing war," "positioned to lead on price," "bidding against Triton for the same refinery and shipyard contracts." Praxion deck: combined entity "#1 in every overlap MSA"; dual-source customers lose competitive bidding. Triton board deck: Praxion is "#1 competitive threat"; Praxion pricing cut Louisiana margins about 350 bps; consolidation "would reduce these customers' negotiating leverage." These are direct evidence of head-to-head price competition and intent to end it. The margin-erosion/overcapacity rationale is not a cognizable defense, and any argument that the parties are not close competitors will be contradicted by their own files.

3.7 Defenses. Entry and national expansion are weak: Air Products and Matheson have no branches in Gulfport-Biloxi or Hattiesburg; Linde has one each; local independents (Gulf States, Dixie) lack bulk, specialty or medical capability; entry takes 12-24 months plus licensing. Efficiencies: the $7.2M branch-consolidation synergy comes from eliminating competition and is not cognizable; the $5.8M procurement and $5.0M G&A savings must be merger-specific, verifiable and passed through - nothing in the record shows pass-through - and $18M against $283M overlap revenue will not rebut a presumption at these concentrations.

4. SPA ISSUES
- Cap (s.6.4(c)-(d)). The cap is aggregate CY2024 revenue of divested, sold or "materially restricted" assets, including revenue "lost or impaired" as a foreseeable result, and applies across Crescent's portfolio. Using workbook branch revenue, divesting the smaller party in each MSA costs: Hattiesburg $9.4M (Praxion), Gulfport-Biloxi $16.1M (Praxion), Mobile $11.6M (Praxion), Baton Rouge $25.8M (Triton), New Orleans $28.5M (Praxion): $91.4M total. Mississippi alone is $25.5M; with Mobile $37.1M (inside the cap); adding Baton Rouge reaches $62.9M (outside). The Praxion deck itself plans closures of branches with $56-71M revenue, which weakens any claim that exit capacity is small and invites a "lost revenue" dispute.
- Reverse fee ($21.25M, 5% of EV). Payable on outside-date termination (s.8.1(b)) or Burdensome Condition termination (s.8.1(d)), not on final-injunction termination (s.8.1(c)) - a drafting gap. With s.8.1(d) (30-day cure) and s.6.4(f) (no duty to litigate), Crescent holds a cheap exit option; sellers will push back, and the "hell-or-high-water" label overstates the covenant.
- Dates. Outside date Oct. 31, 2025, extendable once to Jan. 29, 2026. A Second Request track of 6-12 months (the deal documents' estimate; not independently verified) will exhaust it. As of today both dates have passed; deal status must be confirmed.
- Customer contact (s.6.5(c)) cannot restrict agency outreach; agree a joint customer protocol.
- Gun-jumping. The Praxion integration plan ("immediately upon signing," Rennick chairing, Triton workstream leads) and shared customer-level data risk violating HSR s.7A (15 U.S.C. s.18a) and Sherman Act s.1 before closing. Praxion and Triton remain competitors until close: no joint pricing, bidding or customer allocation; clean-team limits on pricing and customer data.

5. RECOMMENDED STRATEGY
1. Today: litigation hold covering Rennick, Trinh, Dunleavy, Okafor, Hargrove, the Castellanos and both banks/advisors; route analysis through counsel; no new unprivileged commentary on pricing or "rationalization."
2. Reconcile shares, HHIs, branch counts, customer spend and market sizes across all documents; have Pinnacle recompute with disclosed methodology. Do not submit inconsistent figures.
3. Correct fee, thresholds, UPE determination and prior-acquisition scope; draft the filing under the form then in effect.
4. File on time (by Apr. 28) or amend s.6.3(a) rather than breach. Log privilege for the Pinnacle and Bledsoe memos (16 C.F.R. 803.3(d)); produce IC memo, Rennick email, synergy deck and Triton board deck.
5. Pre-filing outreach to the likely reviewing agency (FTC, which handled both industrial-gas precedents; clearance-dependent). Lead with a remedy: Hattiesburg, Gulfport-Biloxi and Mobile (about $37M) to an upfront buyer holding FDA registration and Mississippi/Alabama pharmacy licenses. Buyer scarcity is real: Matheson and AirGas South lack medical licenses.
6. Louisiana contingency: Baton Rouge is presumptively unlawful (37.8% bulk on the workbook, 42% in the narrative); price a Baton Rouge divestiture ($25.8M) and decide whether to seek a cap increase (about $100M covers all five smaller-party divestitures) or rely on s.8.1(d).
7. Advocacy: customer-by-customer, MSA-level evidence; no statewide arguments; drop efficiency claims built on branch closures.
8. Timing: use pull-and-refile once; seek a timing agreement; extend the outside date to at least 12 months.
9. Gun-jumping and clean-team protocol before any integration work; engage state AGs early.
10. Assess litigation readiness, since the SPA does not require Crescent to litigate.

6. OPEN ITEMS
Fund III/IV control structure; actual Coastal Air & Gas size; deal status and any refiling after the Feb. 2026 vacatur; whether early termination is currently available; verified texts of the claimed DOJ 2022 clearance and Guideline 8; branch-level medical revenue.
